label: A hands-on workshop · Avalanche Fuji
notes: Welcome people who have never coded as well as people who have. This is a live workshop, not a promise that AI makes software risk-free. The goal is a small working dApp and a repeatable way to direct an agent.

title:
What happens
after you click?
subtitle: Enough blockchain to understand your first dApp.
notes: Bridge from AI to the software we are going to build. Avoid a long history of cryptocurrencies or investment discussion.

title: A familiar website
footer: Usually, an organization operates the service and its database.
notes: Use a familiar example such as a loyalty-point balance. This is a simplified web application; not every system has exactly three components.

title: A blockchain is a shared record
subtitle: Many computers check updates using common rules.
footer: A public record can be checked beyond one website.
notes: Blocks connect to earlier blocks using cryptographic references. Nodes maintain and verify the chain under a consensus protocol. A blockchain does not prove that every real-world claim written into it is true. Public addresses are pseudonymous, not automatically private.

title: A transaction requests a change
footer: A transaction hash identifies the request. A successful receipt confirms its outcome.
notes: Sending a request is not the same as success. It may be rejected, remain pending or execute and revert. An included failed transaction can still consume gas. Our app waits for a receipt before reporting a successful mint.

title: A smart contract holds the rules
subtitle: Think of a vending machine with inspectable instructions.
items: Request one NFT and pay the mint price
Correct payment? Supply available? Not paused?
Create a token and record its owner
footer: The rules are code. Code can contain mistakes.
notes: The vending-machine analogy is limited: a smart contract executes in the blockchain environment. This repository uses a non-upgradeable contract; changing its bytecode requires a new deployment. Its owner can still change settings explicitly exposed by the code, such as pause and the metadata base URI. Avoid saying every blockchain contract is immutable in every possible sense.

title: Proof of stake: who helps validate?
items: Check blocks and participate in consensus
footer: Exact rewards and penalties depend on the network.
notes: Keep this conceptual. Proof of stake is about participation and economic security; a separate consensus protocol determines agreement. Do not teach Ethereum's specific penalties as universal Avalanche behavior. We are not setting up validators or staking funds in this workshop.

title: Avalanche: ask a sample, repeat
subtitle: Validators repeatedly sample other validators to reach agreement.
footer: Simplified view of Snowman consensus · valid blocks only
notes: Advance through the highlighted nodes. This is an illustrative diagram, not a simulation of protocol thresholds or timing. Stake influences participation; repeated sampling is the agreement mechanism. Invalid transactions are not made valid by votes. Omit performance numbers and detailed parameters.

title: Our classroom: Avalanche Fuji
items: The test network we use today
The chain ID to check in your wallet
footer: Gas is paid in test AVAX. No real funds needed.
notes: Ethereum compatibility lets us use familiar Solidity contracts, ethers and wallet tooling. Fuji is a separate test network. A chain ID tells the app which chain is selected; an address alone does not identify a network. Network details are listed in the appendix.

title: Your wallet is a key manager
footer: MetaMask is one way to interact with your accounts.
notes: For the account model used in this workshop, the private key authorizes signatures. The wallet displays chain data; the NFT is not a picture stored inside the wallet. Never ask anyone to show a secret or recovery phrase during the demonstration.

title: Public address. Private control.
right: Never paste a recovery phrase into AI
Never share your main-wallet private key
footer: The deploy lesson uses a separate, fresh testnet-only burner.
notes: The recovery phrase can restore control over accounts; the app does not need it. The only taught file-based key exception is a fresh disposable testnet-only burner in gitignored foundry/.env. Do not display the .env file in the presentation or screen share. This deck does not connect to a wallet.

title: Three requests. Different meanings.
items: Share the selected account with the site.
Authorize or attest to the displayed message.
Request an on-chain action; gas may be charged.
footer: Read every request. A gas-free signature can still grant important permissions.
notes: Connecting alone is not a token-spending approval. Message signatures can have consequences, including authorizing later actions. Disconnecting a dApp does not revoke previously granted token approvals. Our NFT mint uses native test AVAX rather than an ERC-20 allowance.

title: One mint, step by step
footer: Use Next to reveal each step. This is an illustration, not a real transaction.
notes: Walk through the same journey students will perform. Between the wallet and chain, an RPC endpoint relays requests. The app then reads updated contract data. No wallet connection or network transaction happens in this slide.

title: Mint price and gas are different
footer: Two NFTs cost 0.02 test AVAX plus gas. Gas varies.
notes: The contract requires the exact mint payment for the chosen quantity. The wallet estimates the network fee separately. Rejecting a wallet request before broadcast does not send a transaction; a transaction included but reverted can still consume gas.

title: Checkpoint: get ready to build
items: Use a workshop account; keep recovery information private.
Use the faucet and check your balance.
footer: faucet.avax.network · backup: faucets.chain.link/fuji
notes: Pause here. Install MetaMask only through its official website and official extension-store listing. Follow docs/02-fuji-faucet.md for setup. Faucet availability and eligibility may vary; ask a facilitator if blocked. Never buy real tokens for this workshop.

title:
Make something
you can use.
subtitle: A small NFT minting app. A repeatable way to build.
notes: Show the destination before the tools. If possible, briefly demonstrate a working facilitator dApp in a separate browser tab.

title: Your first dApp
subtitle: A minting page for your own collection.
items: A receipt and your owned tokens
footer: 100 tokens maximum · 0.01 test AVAX each · Fuji only
notes: The visual is a conceptual preview using the repository's fallback art, not a screenshot or a live mint interface. The existing app has a gallery, quantity selector, minted count and My NFTs. Contract address wiring is required before a real mint. Artwork display additionally depends on reachable metadata.

title: The pieces you are connecting
footer: Foundry builds, tests and deploys the contract.
notes: A dApp means decentralized application, but not every part is decentralized. The website and metadata can still use ordinary hosting. ethers talks to the blockchain through an RPC provider and requests wallet signing for transactions. Foundry is development tooling, not part of the user's mint click.

title:
ERC = Ethereum
Request for Comments
subtitle: Shared standards help different apps speak the same language.
footer: 20 and 721 identify different standards, not software versions.
notes: ERCs are a category of standards proposals. ERC-20 and ERC-721 define common token interfaces. Ethereum-compatible chains such as Avalanche C-Chain can implement them too. A standard helps compatibility; it does not guarantee safety, value or support in every wallet.

title: ERC-20: interchangeable units
subtitle: Like points in the same loyalty program.
footer: The question is “how much?” · units of the same token are interchangeable
notes: The analogy is to units within one token contract; different ERC-20 tokens are not interchangeable with each other. ERC-20 includes balance, transfer and allowance interfaces. This repository has WorkToken as an optional extension, not the main build.

title: ERC-721: individually identified tokens
subtitle: Like numbered tickets, each with its own identity.
footer: The question is “which one?” · contract address + token ID identify the NFT on a chain
notes: NFT means non-fungible token. ERC-721 tracks and transfers ownership of individual token IDs. Images are commonly referenced through metadata and are not necessarily stored on-chain. NFT ownership does not automatically transfer copyright or guarantee the truth of a real-world claim.

title: Which standard fits?
right: An owner for each token ID
footer: Choose the behavior first. Choose the standard second.
notes: Ask the audience to classify loyalty points and numbered collectibles. Do not introduce prices or trading. The main workshop stays with ERC-721.

title: Direct the agent with a specification
footer: The learner makes the decisions. The agent helps make them work.
notes: This is the repository's lightweight speckit method. Start from a requirements brief and answer the open questions yourself. The specification is the agreement; implementation is checked against it. Do not ask the agent to invent your collection identity.

title: Your first brief: four decisions
items: Name your collection and describe who it is for.
Choose a theme, colors and artwork.
Connect, mint on Fuji, show ownership and a receipt.
footer: 04 / Leave out payments with real funds, trading and extra features.
notes: Give students a few minutes. Have them answer the R2 brief's open questions; at least three learner answers are required before their spec is written. Fallback art exists in app/public/art. Art creation can be an optional extension if time is short.

title: A prompt that starts a conversation
quote: Read AGENTS.md and requirements/R2-mint-dapp.md. Help me specify my collection. Ask one question at a time. Wait for my confirmation before building.
footer: Your answers become speckit/specs/build-spec.md.
notes: This is a suggested starting prompt, not a completed student specification. After the spec is confirmed, ask for a plan and numbered tasks. Ask the agent to explain unfamiliar terms in one plain paragraph.

title: First checkpoint: a page you can see
footer: Run from the repository root · open http://localhost:3000
notes: Assume installation was completed before the workshop. If verification fails, have the agent inspect the exact error; follow docs/00-setup.md. Starting the frontend is not deployment. A contract-address placeholder is expected until the deploy station. Confirm art and layout in the real page.

title: Give feedback the agent can act on
right: The hero image is stretched. Preserve its proportions.
Show a clear error when the wallet is on the wrong network.
footer: Describe what happened, what you expected, and the smallest change.
notes: Ask students to inspect the real page after each task. Change only what the feedback names. When an error occurs, provide the error text without secrets; do not paste .env files.

title: Read the contract as product rules
footer: The owner can pause minting and change the metadata base URI.
notes: Read foundry/src/MyNFT.sol together. The supply, price and quantity limit are constants in this implementation. Pause and base URI are explicitly mutable owner settings. The owner can also withdraw mint proceeds. The contract is not automatically safe because AI generated code or tests passed.

title: Test before any deployment
commands: Compile and run the contract tests
footer: Green tests are a checkpoint, not a security audit.
notes: The root npm test command runs forge test --root foundry -vv. Do not hard-code a test count: the repo also contains ERC-20 tests. Students should know which behavior is tested. Stop deployment if tests fail.

title: Deploy with a fresh testnet burner
items: Use a fresh, disposable testnet-only wallet.
Its deploy key goes only in gitignored foundry/.env.
After tests pass, run npm run deploy from the root.
footer: Never use the main wallet's key. Never share the .env file or commit it.
notes: Follow docs/05-deploy-foundry.md section 0 and foundry/.env.example privately. Do not show or request any key in the chat or projected screen. The facilitator must verify Fuji before broadcast. The presenter runs no deployment through this HTML deck.

title: Give the website the contract address
footer: A wallet address and a contract address can both start with 0x. Use the deployed contract's address.
notes: Keep the network set to Fuji. The initial all-zero address is a placeholder. Confirm the code at the address and the network before wiring. The address is public; it is not a secret. Finish the wiring specification and verify the frontend reads the deployed supply.

title: Mint. Then prove it happened.
items: Connect on Fuji, choose one NFT and click Mint.
Check the network, contract, payment and gas.
Check success and ownership on testnet.snowtrace.io.
footer: A working button is useful. A confirmed on-chain result is the proof.
notes: Wait for confirmation. Check the transaction status, contract address, mint event and recipient. Confirm the token appears in My NFTs. Missing artwork can mean metadata is unavailable, even when ownership is correct. Localhost images are not accessible to a remote wallet; follow the go-live materials later to host metadata.

title: When it gets stuck
items: Check the extension, connection and pending requests.
Get faucet funds for the mint price and gas.
Check address wiring first; check metadata separately.
footer: Copy the exact error. Explain what you expected. Change one thing.
notes: A rejected request can be retried after review. A failed transaction should be inspected before retrying. If local setup blocks the class, use the facilitator demonstration and complete the environment setup afterward. Avoid destructive resets of student work.

title:
You direct.
The agent builds.
You verify.
subtitle: Today: one small dApp. Next: your own idea.
footer: Describe → build → inspect → refine
notes: Ask someone to explain the mint journey in their own words. Invite students to share their collection page and successful Fuji transaction. Optional next steps are WorkToken and public hosting, using the repository's separate briefs and explicit approvals.
